note: Assertions in this repo's own tests that read source text instead of running it. Real, and standing: tests/test_chain_integrity.py's test_argv_does_not_resolve_off_path asserts a string is absent from kernel/runner.py, which passes for any rewrite of the same bug and fails for a harmless refactor. Written down rather than fixed in the same breath as the checker that found them: each one needs a behavioural test to replace it, which is work, not a rename. Nothing new joins this list without a signature. Narrowed from 27 ids to 18 on 2026-08-10: the rule took every string in the enclosing function, so one unrelated .py literal made every read_text in that function a finding. The 9 that left were never real.

accepted.why: tests/test_what_guards_the_guards.py::test_the_size_is_asked_before_an_unbounded_write — reads kernel/ledger.py and asserts `_seal_if_full` appears before `open("w")` inside `export_jsonl`. It is a claim about the order of two statements, and nothing executable separates the orders until an export exceeds SEAL_AT = 25,000,000 bytes: below that the seal is a no-op either way, and above it the difference is one segment boundary in a 49 MB file. The property it guards is why the sealed segment on disk is 1.97x the number, which is recorded in the comment beside the constant. Two of the three source assertions in this class were converted rather than accepted — `_seal_if_full` is now called for real, with a small `seal_at`, in three cases covering a file under the limit, one over it, and no file at all. This is the one that had nothing to call.

tests/test_what_guards_the_guards.py::test_the_decision_is_written_beside_the_pattern — asserts `chose not to ask` appears in tests/run_without_silent_skips.py. What it holds is that the decision is written down next to the pattern that implements it, and a comment's existence has no behavioural surface by construction: the runner behaves identically whether or not the reason is beside the regex, which is exactly the failure it is there to prevent. The behaviour half is the two cases immediately above it, which put six real reason strings to `runner_mod.ENVIRONMENT` and pin which are quiet and which stay loud.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_both_hooks_ask_the_owner — asserts neither hook carries its own `sqlite3.connect` for the open-task question. That is a claim about there being one copy, and behaviour cannot make it: two copies that both work answer identically, which is the state this repo was in until one of them was found opening the database outside its `try`. The behaviour half is beside it -- a file that is not a database, put to `_framework.is_open`.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_the_stand_in_carries_what_the_hook_reaches_for — asserts both `ImportError` fallbacks name `record_seen` and `is_open`. Running it means making the kernel import fail and reaching the path that calls them, which the case beside it does at the level that has a mechanical answer: both hooks still print `{}` and exit 0. What this holds is that the stand-in and the thing it stands in for have not drifted apart again.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_no_second_literal_survives_in_the_run_paths — asserts `_run` carries no second timeout literal. The behavioural cases beside it prove the number now comes from one owner in all three states (default, declared, sentinel); this one holds that a fourth spelling has not been added back, and a literal that agrees with the constant is invisible to behaviour until the day it stops agreeing.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_a_detector_that_wrote_nothing_adds_no_key — asserts the `out` key is conditional. The row is asserted for real beside it, read back from this repo's own ledger after a live derive; what this adds is the absent-key half, which would need a detector that writes no `--out` in a fixture repo to observe, and reads as identical either way to anything that only looks at rows which have one.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_the_writer_names_the_kind_the_reader_selects — reads kernel/review.py and kernel/sweep.py to hold the writer and the reader of a `lens_reviewed` row to one answer for "which value means no task". Behaviour cannot see that agreement: each side is correct alone, and they disagree only about a row one writes and the other queries. The behavioural half is three cases in tests/test_the_brief_a_reviewer_can_follow.py, which write both rows against a real ledger and read `task_id` back. Moved here from that file, and the move is the point: `redgreen.verify` parses the whole closing-test file, so one source assertion anywhere in it means the file can never close a review finding -- measured, exit 1, "asserts on the source text of the code it is closing".

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_both_writers_normalise_an_empty_task — counts the normalisation in both writers rather than one. The sibling file proves each writer stores NULL; this holds that neither was left behind when the rule was applied, and two functions being individually right is exactly the state a partial repair leaves.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::test_the_lens_check_still_needs_a_corpus — pins the condition `if lens and usable and lens not in usable`. The first spelling omitted `usable` and refused every finding in a repo with no lens files at all; the existing suite caught it. In a repo that has lenses the two spellings behave identically, so nothing executable distinguishes the correction from the mistake.

tests/test_what_the_output_says_it_did.py::test_review_close_says_it_has_not_been_checked — reads kernel/cli.py and asserts the closure offer prints that it has not been verified. Running it means raising a real finding claim, binding a closing test to it, and capturing stdout, in order to check a print statement — a fabricated finding testing a sentence written in the same commit. Three of the five source assertions in this file were converted rather than accepted: `risk.attribution` was extracted so three tests call it with an agent record, a person record and a pre-field record, and the two status numbers are read from a real `bin/v4 status --json` run. These two are what is left.

tests/test_what_the_output_says_it_did.py::test_and_names_the_command_that_gives_the_verdict — the same print, asserting it names `ledger.REVIEW_TASK` rather than describing a condition. Separate from the one above because they are two claims about one line and merging them would go green when either half alone survived. The behavioural half of this class is `test_and_names_the_command_that_gives_the_verdict`'s second assertion, which calls nothing but reads the constant: `REVIEW_TASK == 'repo-review'` is checked against the module, not against the file.

tests/test_a_language_the_tracer_can_read.py::test_the_closing_gate_asks_rather_than_spelling_it — reads checkers/review_finding.py and asserts it calls `redgreen.traceable` rather than spelling `endswith(".py")` itself. It calls nothing, and behaviour cannot replace it: a second copy of "which languages can be traced" answers identically to the owner until it drifts, which is precisely what happened here — the tracer gained Go and Node and this file went on refusing everything but Python, giving a reason about `sitecustomize` that had stopped being true. The eleven cases beside it in the same file do run: they call `traceable`, `resolve_symbol` and the checker itself, and pin exits 0, 1 and 4.

tests/test_a_language_the_tracer_can_read.py::test_and_so_does_the_command_that_refuses_a_symbol — the same assertion against kernel/review.py, which carried the second copy. Kept separate from the one above rather than merged: they are two files that drifted independently, and a single test covering both would go green when either one alone was repaired. `resolve_symbol` still reads `.py` a few lines further down, for whether a Python AST can be run over the file, and that is a different question which behaviour does cover — `test_python_normalisation_is_untouched` and `test_and_a_module_level_constant_is_still_refused` call it.

tests/test_a_landmark_in_a_language_the_checker_reads.py::test_every_site_reads_the_same_owner — reads kernel/spec_coverage.py and asserts no site spells a past-run mark of its own. It never calls anything, and there is nothing behavioural to replace it with: `當時 in line or 前身 in line` at three sites and `_about_the_past(line)` at three sites answer identically for every input, so no execution can tell them apart. That is exactly how the third site came to be missing `V3` and `rev 1` while the other two had them — the divergence was invisible to behaviour, and the test that would have caught it is this one. The three cases beside it in the same class do run: they call `_about_the_past` on each mark and on three sentences that must not be exempt.

tests/test_kernel.py::test_a_value_the_repo_chose_is_left_alone — the same over-reach as c97e789dde05c58e. It reads back the JSON the test itself just wrote, and the rule fires because `.py` string literals (`my_lint.py`, `always_lint.py` — detector filenames, which is what the assertion is about) sit beside a `read_text`. Nothing here asserts on source text; the file being read is this test's own output.

tests/test_kernel.py::test_the_marker_the_writer_writes_is_the_one_the_reader_matches — asserts the writer does not spell the marker a second time. Same shape: a second literal would pass every behavioural case above it in the same test, which is why the source check is there.

tests/test_kernel.py::test_no_v4_path_falls_between_the_two_sets — parses kernel/cli.py to find every `stamp_generated` call site. The source IS the subject: the question is whether any `.v4/` path is answered for by neither route, and that is a fact about the code's shape, not about what a call returns. Nothing to execute instead.

tests/test_secret_scan.py::_module — not an assertion at all. It execs the top of checkers/secret_scan.py to import the half above `def inspect(`, because the file shadows the builtin. The checker reads any source-file read inside a test as this shape; this one is a loader. Worth noting as the rule's one known over-reach here.

tests/test_rust_without_a_rust_parser.py::test_a_checker_that_reads_neither_rust_nor_go_is_unmoved — the `read_text` is a probe, not an assertion: it saves the Go emitter's bytes, appends a line, recomputes `hashing.program_sha` for a checker that reads neither Rust nor Go, asserts the sha did not move, and restores the file in `addCleanup`. Nothing in the file asserts on source text. Signed `baseline_raise` eight times across fw-rust, fw-lens and five more before anyone wrote it down -- the file it belongs in has existed the whole time.

tests/test_kernel.py::test_and_no_tracked_v4_file_falls_between_them_either -- `ast.parse(kernel/cli.py)` to collect the literals passed to `stamp_generated`, which is the third of the four ways a `.v4/` path can be accounted for. The sibling case above it does exactly this and is already accepted here (8743928cb49df5d7's neighbours); reading it a second way would put two answers on one question, which is the shape the finding this case closes (d52045d6d41c852c) is about.

It cannot be asked by running: that call executes only inside `v4 install`, and running install against an installed repo overwrites the repo's own files. The alternative -- reading `.v4/installed.json` for the three shas -- would be a test that goes red because a manifest is stale, which is an environment fact and not a claim about the code.

What is asserted around it is not source text: the case runs `git ls-files .v4` and requires every tracked entry to be in one of the four sets. That half is what makes it a test; this half is how it learns what the fourth set holds.

tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py::ADoctorCheckReadsEverythingItComputes::test_it -- `ast.parse(kernel/doctor.py)` to find every name assigned inside `_check_a_registered_checker_that_has_never_executed` and never read. A dead local is invisible to behaviour by definition: the function returns the same verdict for every input whether or not the `DISTINCT` query above it is read, which is exactly why it survived under five lines of comment explaining what it decided. The behavioural half is beside it in tests/test_checks_that_answered_from_nothing.py, which asks the check for a verdict.

This one is not new and it is not this task's. The file is byte-identical at 0587058, eight of its nine findings were already on this list, and 7a7a52b moved this assertion into the file without adding the ninth. That commit's own message says why it moved it: "redgreen.verify parses the whole closing-test file" -- the defect 918d717f names and the change landing beside this entry repairs. The workaround shipped; the line that would have made it legible did not.

Found by a task whose scope did not include this file, and written down here rather than repaired in passing: converting it needs a behavioural replacement that does not exist, which is work, not a rename.

2026-09-06, later the same day: a ninth entry for tests/test_two_modules_that_have_to_agree.py, which is where this repo keeps the assertions it has decided read source on purpose. Eight of its nine were already here; 7a7a52b moved the ninth in and did not list it, so `test-shape` has been one finding short of green on that file since.
